#### Analyzing the Score Change: Overcoming Platform Bottlenecks

The live readings above compare the Google Sites origin (`sites.google.com/view/...`) with the same site served through the edge. The origin ships heavy platform JavaScript and render-blocking CSS, which hurts mobile most. The Worker changes how the page is delivered, and these are the main differences to look for in the readings:

- **Render-Blocking Mitigation (LCP):** The edge swaps the render-blocking Google stylesheet for an R2-hosted copy (deferred on mobile) and preloads the LCP image, so mobile LCP and FCP should be clearly lower than the origin's. The size of the gap changes between PSI runs.
- **Main-Thread Offloading (TBT):** Total Blocking Time and the Performance score move the most, because platform scripts are the main source of blocking on the origin. These are lab (Lighthouse) results, not field data.
- **Technical SEO Fixes:** The origin loses SEO points for missing meta description, heading hierarchy, canonical and structured data. The edge injects all of them. A perfect Lighthouse SEO score is a checklist result, not a ranking guarantee.

This **proof of concept (PoC)** points to a pattern in the modern, AI-driven web. The underlying CMS you build on matters far less than the network layer that serves it. Crawlers and autonomous LLM engines only index what they are permitted to parse. Ultimately, whoever controls the doorways—the Edge—shapes what machines read.

## Indexation Evidence: A Baseline Parsing Test

Google Sites puts the real content inside a sandboxed iframe. A lot of AI crawlers never see it cleanly, and even Google often treats iframe content as belonging to the frame URL, not the parent page. The edge layer turns that content into plain, structured HTML.

The rule is simple: same text, same facts, same links for every lane. Only the packaging changes. That is how you stay on the right side of dynamic rendering instead of sliding into cloaking.

- **Layer 1: Human visitors.** Full interactive UI, iframe unboxed via `srcdoc`, scripts delayed until real interaction.
- **Layer 2: Search crawlers (Googlebot, Bingbot, etc.).** Origin HTML plus the same ghost text block prepended. Nothing stripped.
- **Layer 3: AI agents and social bots.** Clean, stripped ghost payload only — same text and facts, no origin bloat.

You can check the AI-agent lane with [`?debug=bot`](https://www.eryc.my.id/case-studies/edge-seo?debug=bot) and the search-crawler lane with [`?debug=googlebot`](https://www.eryc.my.id/case-studies/edge-seo?debug=googlebot). Note: the URL Inspection fetcher’s User-Agent may receive the human layer instead — see the [GSC Render Comparison](#two-lanes).

### What the data shows

Search Console shows impressions for queries matching this content:

- **Commercial:**
  `advance technical seo indonesia`,
  `edge seo specialist indonesia`,
  `geo specialist malang`,
  `edge seo malang`
- **Architecture and brand:**
  `asymmetric ghost payload`,
  `eryc seo`,
  `eryc agp`

Ranking for low-competition or coined terms is not a ranking claim. The useful signal is indexation: the text is now readable at all. On the native Google Sites URL the same content sits behind the iframe wall. Side-by-side URL Inspection is a cleaner test than raw search visibility:

- Edge layer off: *Render blocked by iframe sandbox (Oct 2026)*
- Edge layer on: *Full HTML structure and JSON-LD parsed natively (Oct 2026)*

### Working hypothesis: signal density over volume

This site has only a handful of pages. The hypothesis is simple: a clean, structured, noise-free entity graph served as readable HTML can be understood without hundreds of supporting pages. One site, one test. Treat it as a hypothesis to be replicated, not a final conclusion.

## Verdict: A Working Proof of Concept

This experiment was built to answer one question: can a platform that crawlers cannot read be made machine-readable from the network layer alone? Here is what the result shows, in order, including where it stops.

### 1. Machine Readability Comes First

**Conviction:** Machine readability comes first. If the page cannot be cleanly parsed, nothing else matters — not content quality, not links, not brand. Ranking and citation both require the content to be readable in the first place. The edge approach does not wait for the crawler to struggle with iframes or missing structure. It supplies a clean, structured version at the network layer. That is the minimum requirement. Everything else is secondary.

**Observed:** The gap is observable. Both the native Google Sites URL and the edge domain are tracked in Search Console, so the difference can be inspected side by side (see the GSC render comparisons above). The edge layer is a per-page function, so a larger site changes how many times it runs, not what it does.

### 2. The Constraint Stack

The experiment was deliberately run under the hardest combination of conditions I could find, all at once:

- **Platform:** Google Sites, which offers no control over meta tags, canonicals, robots.txt, sitemap or structured data. The edge layer adds that whole control surface (robots.txt, sitemap.xml, llms.txt, canonical, JSON-LD) without touching the CMS.
- **Experience:** a fully interactive interface with an animated background, not a stripped-down page.
- **Performance:** a PSI score of 99 (lab data, not field data; current numbers are in Live Telemetry).
- **Domain:** .my.id, a TLD that starts with no inherited trust.
- **Infrastructure:** hosted on Google's infrastructure and fronted by Cloudflare's (TLS, DDoS protection, caching). The iframe sandbox and CSP are relaxed only for content I control.
- **Cost:** under $1 a year for the domain, plus the free tiers of Google Sites and Cloudflare. The real cost was time — months of deliberate work under hard constraints.

**Observed:** Most of the complexity comes from two constraints: a locked CMS (no access to head tags or page structure, so everything is injected from outside) and a PSI score of 99 under a heavy animated background (hence the deferred hydration and cron-maintained visual state). *Hypothesis: Astro or Next.js would remove much of that work, since server rendering and selective hydration are defaults there. Untested.*

### 3. Why Clicks Are the Wrong Scoreboard

**Observed (as of October 17, 2026):** Cloudflare counted 5.17k visits in the last 30 days. Search Console recorded 20 clicks in the 28 days from September 17 to October 14. Google clicks are well under 1% of the activity.

Clicks and CTR were built for a human scanning ten blue links. More and more readers are machines that never click, and humans arriving via AI answers behave differently. So this experiment asks a different question: can machines parse this page? I measure that with things you can check yourself: what a bot receives with `?debug=bot`, what Search Console renders, and whether the page gets indexed. Citation is the next scoreboard, and nobody has a tool for it yet.

**Limit:** those visits include my own testing and automation. The gap shows click metrics miss most activity, not that bots are the majority. Site size only scales the counts; the measurement is the same on any site.

### 4. The Limits

- **Content quality still matters.** Machine readability solves ingestion and token limits. Traditional SEO still applies.
- **Fundamentals decide the outcome.** Helpful content and user experience are what drive crawl demand. The edge cannot fake them.
- **Payloads are hand-built per page.** Each page needs its own KV entry plus a parity check. The cron AI Worker only maintains visual state (LCP image URL, background color); it does not write payloads. Automatic generation is the goal of the open-source build (see [What Comes Next](#next)).
- **Hypothesis:** the edge code scales, since it runs per request, and generated payloads would extend it to many similar pages.
- **Parity is a standing obligation.** The ghost version must keep the same text content as the human version. If the two drift apart, it stops being dynamic rendering and becomes cloaking. Because the ghost HTML is a separate, hand-maintained copy, I run a text-parity check against the rendered page before each KV write (outside the Worker, which does not check at request time). You can compare it yourself: open the page normally, then with `?debug=bot`, and diff the visible text. Expect two known differences: live telemetry numbers exist only in the human layer (the ghost copy shows placeholders), and the ghost copy carries short bracketed notes where the human layer renders interactive components.
- **Lighthouse/PSI is special-cased.** Runs identified by User-Agent skip the script wake-up and the heavy-background upgrade, so lab scores describe that variant. Real-user (field) data is the check that matters.
- **Hypothesis: the risk is contained and reversible.** Remove the Worker and purge the cache. *I'd be wrong if* the origin still shows edge-injected changes after rollback.

### 5. What This Contributes

Everything below runs in production on this page and can be checked with the debug lanes and the validator:

- **Iframe unboxing at the edge:** the Google Sites embed is rewritten into inline `srcdoc` HTML, so its content is part of the document instead of hidden behind a sandboxed iframe.
- **Lane-based delivery:** one URL, different packaging for humans, search crawlers and AI agents, with the text intended to stay the same and a query-parameter debug flag for each bot lane.
- **KV-backed ghost payloads:** per-path structured HTML (H1→H3 plus a JSON-LD @graph) served from edge storage, with a decoupled cron worker maintaining visual state so no AI runs at request time.
- **Interaction-triggered hydration:** native scripts are deferred until real interaction to keep the main thread free.
- **Verification surfaces:** a validator terminal, `?debug=bot`, `?debug=googlebot` and a documented parity obligation, so each claim can be checked instead of trusted.

Architecturally, this is a strangler-fig-style approach: an edge layer in front of an untouched origin that upgrades pages one at a time, while unmigrated pages pass through as before. Unlike the classic pattern, the origin is never retired. It stays the source of truth. That is also why hand-written payloads are acceptable at this stage: each page can be migrated independently.

I am not aware of a public implementation that combines these for a locked CMS, though I have not done an exhaustive survey. It required distributed-systems work: an edge Worker, a decoupled cron worker, and asynchronous KV state.

### 6. What Comes Next: Open-Source, CMS-Agnostic Agent Readability

The real problem is bigger than Google Sites. Some crawlers still struggle with JavaScript. Retrieval pipelines differ. New agents keep appearing. You cannot chase every query. What you can engineer is how easy the page is to ingest cleanly.

Next step is to turn this from a single-site, hand-maintained prototype into an open-source, CMS-agnostic tool. The goal is simple: let people focus on useful content while the edge handles the machine-readable layer. No release date yet — still looking for the resources to build it properly.

The Google Sites deployment is the stress test: the approach working from outside a locked CMS. **Hypothesis:** the production target is [EmDash](https://github.com/emdash-cms/emdash), a full-stack TypeScript CMS built on Astro and Cloudflare Workers. There the edge can be the origin, so no mid-flight interception or iframe unboxing is needed, and humans and bots can receive the same structured HTML, which removes the parity risk. EmDash is in beta preview, so this is a direction to test, not a proven result.

**What needs to exist:**

- **Ghost-payload generator:** builds the structured, parity-checked bot copy from the rendered page (no more hand-written KV entries).
- **Parity checker:** diffs human and bot text and blocks the write when they drift.
- **Crawler behavior matrix:** a public, log-based record of how different agents actually behave.
- **CMS adapters:** validation on at least two platforms beyond Google Sites.

**Proposed success measures:** parity pass rate, tokens per page before and after, and a citation-test protocol with a larger prompt set across several engines, so the hypothesis that fewer tokens means more citation opportunity is tested rather than assumed. If you want to support or sponsor it, [get in touch](mailto:eryc.me@gmail.com).

> “Judge me by the constraints I can overcome, not just by the platforms I've already mastered.”

In this world, it isn't the big that beat the small, but the fast that beat the slow.
